## Analog activities (90 minutes, no computers)

The whole session acts out one story: **pick a bag, then draw balls**. A bag is
a community, a tissue state, or a patch of forest. A ball is a read, a fragment,
or an animal you spotted. Any study that fits that story produces a count table,
and everything this week works on count tables.

The first fifty minutes are on your feet. The last thirty-five are pen and paper.
The slides for every step are at the end of this afternoon's deck.

### Materials

| item | how many | used for |
|---|---|---|
| Opaque cloth or paper bags | 4 | demo |
| Pom-poms in 8 colours | about 50 per bag | demo |
| Felt-tip markers in the same 8 colours | 2 sets | demo cards |
| Blank cards, `D____` | 12 | demo |
| Printed sample cards, `S01` to `S80` | 1 per participant | rounds 1 and 2, worksheet |
| Worksheet, printed double-sided | 1 per participant, plus spares | build the table |
| Masking tape | 1 roll | floor axes |
| Flip chart and marker | 1 | report to the room |
| Whiteboard and marker | 1 | dendrogram in round 1 |

### Before the session

**Fill the four bags** with about 50 pom-poms each, and tag each bag with its
inflammation status.

| bag | orange | green | blue | pink | vermillion | sky blue | yellow | grey | tag |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 42 | 4 | 1 | | 1 | | 1 | 1 | low |
| 2 | 4 | 38 | 4 | | 1 | | 1 | 2 | low |
| 3 | 1 | 4 | 35 | | 4 | 2 | 2 | 2 | high |
| 4 | | 1 | 9 | 23 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 2 | high |

**Tape the floor axes** in an open part of the room: one long line left to right
(more blue toward the right), and one line front to back crossing it at the left
end (more orange toward the back, more green toward the front).

**Sort the printed cards** in order, `S01` first. The deck is interleaved, so
handing out the first 61 cards still gives a balanced room. Keep the rest as
spares.

### Run sheet

| time | block |
|---|---|
| 0:00 | Bags and balls, live demo |
| 0:12 | Hand out cards |
| 0:15 | Round 1: closest partner, then pairs of pairs |
| 0:27 | Round 2: the floor is a plot |
| 0:37 | Reveal and debrief |
| 0:45 | Build the table, worksheet |
| 1:20 | Report to the room |
| 1:25 | Close |

### Bags and balls (12 min)

Put the four bags on a table at the front and ask for eight volunteers, two per
bag. Without looking, the first person at each bag draws **5** pom-poms and the
second draws **20**. Each tallies their colours on the back of a blank card,
colours the bar on the front, and copies the bag's inflammation tag. Hold the
pairs of cards up side by side.

Ask the room:

- Did the two people at the same bag make the same card?
- Which of the two cards do you trust more? Why?
- If the 5-ball card were all you had, what would you conclude about that bag?

> Picking the bag is biology. Drawing the balls is measurement. Every sample
> you will see this week has both kinds of variation in it, and only the second
> one shrinks when you sequence deeper.

### Hand out cards (3 min)

Give everyone one printed card. The eight volunteers keep their hand-made card.
Explain the card on the slide: the front shows proportions, so every bar is the
same length, and the small **n** is how many balls were drawn. The back has the
counts and the inflammation tag. The printed cards came from the same kind of
bags.

### Round 1: closest partner, then pairs of pairs (12 min)

1. Everyone finds the one card most like theirs and stands together.
   Compare bars, not card numbers. A group of three is fine.
2. Each pair finds its closest pair.
3. Each group of four finds its closest group.

While they move, draw the merges on the whiteboard as a tree: two names joined,
then two pairs joined. That drawing is a dendrogram.

Ask the room:

- How did you decide two cards were similar? That rule is a distance.
- When two groups both wanted the same pair, how did you settle it? That choice
  is the linkage rule, and software makes it for you.
- Who had trouble finding a partner? Look at the **n** on their card.

> This is hierarchical clustering. On Wednesday the distance gets a name,
> Bray-Curtis, and the tree gets drawn by a computer.

### Round 2: the floor is a plot (10 min)

Everyone stands where their card belongs on the taped axes: left to right by
how much of the bar is blue, back to front by orange share minus green share.
Take a photo from as high as you can, a chair is enough. The slides have a
precomputed version of the plot if the photo does not work out.

Ask the room:

- The blue and pink cards are standing close together. Are their bars alike?
- We chose these two axes. What would you need to separate everyone properly?

> A PCoA is the computer choosing the axes for you. It finds the directions
> along which the cards differ most, and it reports how much of the difference
> each axis captures.

### Reveal and debrief (8 min)

Go past the spoiler slide. Show which bag each card came from, then the computer
versions of both rounds: the floor plot, the PCoA, and the dendrogram.

Points to pull out:

- Cards with 5 to 10 balls end up in the wrong place more often. Too few reads
  turn into ordination error.
- Blends stand between groups. Real communities shift, and a clustering forces
  each one into a single group anyway.
- Two axes squash the blue and pink bags together. A third axis separates them.

### Build the table (35 min)

People sit with whoever is near them. Groups will be different sizes, and that
is fine. Each person gets a worksheet, and the group pools its cards.

On side 1, everyone copies the group's cards into the columns, one card per
column, and fills the feature metadata from the slide. Point out the layout:
sample information sits above the columns it describes, feature information sits
beside the rows it describes. That alignment is what R has to keep in sync.

Side 2 has the questions. Walk round and push on these two:

- **Collapse the rows.** "Makes lactic acid" plus "encodes lysin" does not equal
  the column total, because green is in both groups. Taxonomy is a hierarchy, so
  every row has one parent and adding up is safe. Gene sets overlap, so one gene
  counts in many sets. That overlap comes back on Thursday.
- **Keep only high inflammation.** Crossing out columns in the counts means
  crossing out the same entries in the sample metadata. Nothing else on the
  sheet changes.

### Report to the room (5 min)

Each group copies its 2 × 2 (mostly lactic acid or not, high or low
inflammation) onto the flip chart with its **n**. Add up the columns for the
room total.

Ask the room:

- Did your table show the pattern the room shows?
- Was any group wrong, or just small?

> Tomorrow afternoon this question gets a number: a p-value, and how it depends
> on n.

### Close (5 min)

Leave the flip chart up. Tomorrow the same table has 220 rows of bacteria or
14,226 rows of human genes, and 471 columns. Everything done by hand today is
one line of R.
